title: A testable project contract and model
goal: Specify an inventory tool whose commands and report can be checked against exact observations.

prerequisites.text: Recall records, a quantity field and key lookup. Prepare a folder for the three project files and records.tsv.

terms.title: Contract
terms.definition: Rules for input, state, results and failure that let you agree on a prediction before running.

terms.title: Invariant
terms.definition: A rule that holds after every accepted operation. Here IDs stay unique and quantities stay in range.

sections.title: Zero belongs to a record
paragraphs: Shelf 20 is empty during a stocktake, yet item 20 still exists in the log. Seven units arrive tomorrow. If a search returns only a quantity, zero cannot tell you whether the item exists. Find the record by ID first and then read its quantity.

The module contract starts with a headerless records.tsv. Each row is an ID from 1 to 9999, one TAB and a quantity from 0 to 9999. A number has 1–4 decimal digits. Leading zeros are accepted, so 0010 and 10 identify the same record. An empty file is valid and there can be up to 64 records. LF separates lines. The final LF is optional.

Enter one command per line in stdin. The forms are find ID, set ID QTY and report, with one space between words. Extra characters and a blank command produce invalid and status 2. An unknown ID produces missing and processing continues. Report writes summary.tsv with a tab-separated id and quantity header, then rows in input order. Every report row ends with LF.
The project invariants are compact: the record count stays within capacity, IDs are unique, and set changes only the quantity of an existing item. The report exposes the state after the commands.

sections.title: Follow three commands and check the report
paragraphs: The file has two rows: item 10 has 5 units and item 20 has none. The three commands below change only record 20. The walkthrough writes example-summary.tsv, keeping summary.tsv for your own work.

Before looking at the code, sketch two rows for the stock state. After each command, mark only the changed field and record the visible message. For report, copy both rows to the file in their previous order. Then repeat with input records arriving in another order.
steps: find 10 finds the first record and prints 10 5.
set 20 7 changes the quantity in the second record and replies ok.
report uses the updated quantities, writes the header and two rows, then prints reported.

sections.title: Where to look for the cause
paragraphs: If find 20 prints missing before the update, check which field determines a match. A zero quantity still belongs in the report. If code refers to counts, check the field name in inventory.h.

sections.title: Test your prediction with a new input
paragraphs: Invent three checks. For an ordinary case, find a present ID. At a boundary, try quantity 0 or ID 9999. For invalid input, predict the last line of stdout and whether a report file will exist.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Compare the listed C17 rules with their use in this project.

selfcheck.prompt: records.tsv contains item 20 with quantity 0. What does find 20 print?
feedback: The syntax and the ID are both valid.

selfcheck.prompt: The file has 64 unique IDs, all with zero stock. How do you check the capacity boundary by adding a 65th unique ID?
options: First check a report with 64 data rows, then run separately with one new row and expect capacity-error.
Repeat one of the existing 64 IDs and expect capacity-error.
Count only nonzero quantities, so this file still has spare capacity.
feedback: The two runs check the accepted boundary and the first value beyond it.
A repeated ID tests uniqueness and gives duplicate-id before the capacity check.
Every record takes a slot, including zero-stock records.

selfcheck.prompt: Predict the rows in summary.tsv for item 99 with quantity 4 followed by item 12 with quantity 0 after set 12 3 and report. Explain the order.
selfcheck.feedback: After the header come 99 with quantity 4 and 12 with quantity 3. Loading order stays intact and the update changes only the quantity.

practice.title: An unsorted tool count
practice.task: Start with records.tsv for items 42 and 7. Complete the report loop after the header. Check the agreed row order. Write down the expected stdout, stderr, status and exact file for two checks before running.

steps.action: Run the starter with the supplied stdin.
steps.why: The commands already work and the separate file exposes what remains.
steps.expected: The console ends with reported and summary.tsv only has a header.

steps.action: Write each row and verify that 42 appears before 7.
steps.why: The report preserves input order and uses the current quantity.
steps.expected: The file contains the header, 42 with quantity 9 and 7 with quantity 2.

criteria: find 42, set 7 2 and report print 42 9, ok and reported. Stderr is empty and status is 0.
summary.tsv has exactly three rows with TAB and LF. An empty inventory produces just the header.
practice.hint: Make a two-row table in load order. Mark the start and end of the report body after the header. Check that the ID and quantity in each row come from the same record.

exercises.title: One more check
exercises.task: Check ID 9999 and quantity 0 separately. Confirm that the report keeps the record and adds the final LF.
criteria: Write your prediction before running. Compare stdout, stderr, status and files.

teaching.scene: A stock operator needs to find items, update quantities, and produce a report. Write down what must remain true after every command and verify it with the output and file.

predict.prompt: records.tsv holds item 10 with quantity 5 and item 20 with quantity 0. What follows find 10, set 20 7, and report? Write the three console lines and the report row order.
predict.answer: stdout contains 10 5, ok, and reported on separate lines. In example-summary.tsv, the header id TAB quantity is followed by 10 TAB 5 and 20 TAB 7. The input row order is preserved. stderr is empty and exit status is 0.

apply.prompt: In a clean copy, reverse the load order: 20 TAB 0 LF, then 10 TAB 5 LF. Run set 20 3, find 10, and report. Which lines appear on the screen, and which lines appear in the file and in what order?
apply.answer: Stdout shows ok, 10 5, and reported. After the id TAB quantity header, the file contains 20 TAB 3 and then 10 TAB 5. The report preserves load order. Looking up a record reads the state without changing that order.

practice.strategy: Record the TSV format and the required row order first. Trace the three commands for IDs 42 and 7 against the inventory state. Write expectations for stdout, stderr, exit status, and the file separately.
practice.diagnosis: If reported appears but the file contains only the header, check whether the report visits any records. If values are correct but out of order, compare traversal order with load order.

syntax.explanation: The loop condition i < count visits only populated records. Both the ID and quantity on a report row come from the same Record.
syntax.mistake: Do not replace the actual count with array capacity. Do not sort the report unless the contract calls for it.
